nameStory: Despite its name, eastern redcedar isn't actually a cedar at all — it's a juniper! Early European settlers called it 'cedar' because its aromatic, rot-resistant wood reminded them of true cedars from the Old World. The 'red' comes from the beautiful reddish heartwood that becomes more pronounced as the tree ages.
description: Eastern redcedar is a small to medium-sized evergreen tree that typically grows 15-40 feet tall with a distinctive narrow, pyramid shape when young. As it matures, it often develops a more irregular, scraggly crown with twisted branches. The tree has two very different types of foliage — sharp, needle-like leaves on young growth and tiny, scale-like leaves that overlap like shingles on mature branches. Its fibrous, reddish-brown bark peels off in long strips.

idTips.label: Foliage Types
idTips.description: Look for both needle-like and scale-like leaves on the same tree — young shoots have sharp, prickly needles while mature branches have tiny scales that feel soft when rubbed the right way, like petting a cat

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Fibrous, reddish-brown bark that peels off in long, shreddy strips — run your fingers along it and it feels soft and stringy, never hard or plated

idTips.label: Berries
idTips.description: Small, blue berries with a waxy coating that makes them look dusty or frosted — they're actually tiny cones and have a strong gin-like smell when crushed

idTips.label: Tree Shape
idTips.description: Young trees form perfect Christmas tree triangles, but older specimens become wonderfully irregular with twisted, gnarled branches reaching in different directions

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Crush the foliage and you'll smell a sharp, clean fragrance — somewhere between gin and pencil shavings with a hint of apple

idTips.label: Wood Color
idTips.description: If you see exposed wood from broken branches, look for the distinctive reddish heartwood surrounded by pale sapwood

habitat: Eastern redcedar thrives in dry, rocky soils and disturbed areas throughout New England, especially in old fields, pastures, and along roadsides. You'll often find it growing on limestone outcrops, abandoned farmland, and coastal areas where salt tolerance is important. It's particularly common in southern New England and becomes less frequent in the northern mountains.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright yellow-green tips on branch ends, and you may notice clouds of yellow pollen being released from male trees on windy days.
seasonality.summer: The tree maintains its evergreen appearance, and small green berry-like cones begin forming on female trees.
seasonality.fall: Berry-cones ripen to blue with a waxy coating, and the tree's reddish bark becomes more noticeable as deciduous trees lose their leaves.
seasonality.winter: The evergreen foliage often takes on bronze or purplish tints in cold weather, and the tree's distinctive silhouette stands out dramatically in the winter landscape.

funFact: Eastern redcedar can live for over 900 years, and some ancient specimens in the Midwest are among the oldest living trees in North America — older than many giant sequoias and bristlecone pines!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with true cedars (like white cedar) or other evergreens, but the combination of both needle and scale leaves on the same tree is your giveaway — no other New England evergreen has this dual personality. Memory trick: 'Two types of leaves means it's a juniper, not a cedar!'
contextualKnowledge: The name confusion runs deep — eastern redcedar is neither red nor a cedar! It's a juniper whose berries are used to flavor gin. True cedars don't grow naturally in North America, so any 'cedar' you find here is likely something else entirely (like this juniper, or white cedar which is actually an arborvitae).
compareHints: Unlike common juniper which stays low and shrubby with only needle-like leaves, eastern redcedar grows into a proper tree with both needle and scale foliage. Creeping juniper stays flat against the ground, while eastern redcedar always grows upright. The other junipers in New England gardens are typically non-native ornamentals that lack the distinctive fibrous, peeling bark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common juniper is easily distinguished from eastern redcedar by its low, spreading growth habit (redcedar grows tall and upright) and its sharp needle-like leaves (redcedar has scale-like leaves that lie flat against branches).
Unlike eastern redcedar which grows tall and upright, or common juniper which forms low but upright shrubs, creeping juniper is the only New England juniper that truly grows flat along the ground.
Temple juniper stands apart from New England's other junipers by its uniquely rigid, sharply pointed needles that radiate in all directions from the branches.
Japanese garden juniper is much lower and more spreading than eastern redcedar, which grows as an upright tree.
